Changes since OpenSSH 4.2:
============================ 

Security bugs resolved in this release:

 * CVE-2006-0225: scp (as does rcp, on which it is based) invoked a
   subshell to perform local to local, and remote to remote copy
   operations. This subshell exposed filenames to shell expansion
   twice; allowing a local attacker to create filenames containing
   shell metacharacters that, if matched by a wildcard, could lead
   to execution of attacker-specified commands with the privilege of
   the user running scp (Bugzilla #1094)

This is primarily a bug-fix release, only one new feature has been
added: 

 * Add support for tunneling arbitrary network packets over a
   connection between an OpenSSH client and server via tun(4) virtual
   network interfaces. This allows the use of OpenSSH (4.3+) to create
   a true VPN between the client and server providing real network
   connectivity at layer 2 or 3. This feature is experimental and is 
   currently supported on OpenBSD, Linux, NetBSD (IPv4 only) and 
   FreeBSD. Other operating systems with tun/tap interface capability 
   may be added in future portable OpenSSH releases. Please refer to 
   the README.tun file in the source distribution for further details
   and usage examples.

Some of the other bugs resolved and internal improvements are:

 * Reduce default key length for new DSA keys generated by ssh-keygen 
   back to 1024 bits. DSA is not specified for longer lengths and does 
   not fully benefit from simply making keys longer. As per FIPS 186-2 
   Change Notice 1, ssh-keygen will refuse to generate a new DSA key 
   smaller or larger than 1024 bits

 * Fixed X forwarding failing to start when a the X11 client is executed
   in background at the time of session exit (Bugzilla #1086)

 * Change ssh-keygen to generate a protocol 2 RSA key when invoked
   without arguments (Bugzilla #1064)

 * Fix timing variance for valid vs. invalid accounts when attempting
   Kerberos authentication (Bugzilla #975)

 * Ensure that ssh always returns code 255 on internal error (Bugzilla 
   #1137)

 * Cleanup wtmp files on SIGTERM when not using privsep (Bugzilla #1029)

 * Set SO_REUSEADDR on X11 listeners to avoid problems caused by
   lingering sockets from previous session (X11 applications can
   sometimes not connect to 127.0.0.1:60xx) (Bugzilla #1076)

 * Ensure that fds 0, 1 and 2 are always attached in all programs, by
   duping /dev/null to them if necessary.

 * Xauth list invocation had bogus "." argument (Bugzilla #1082)

 * Remove internal assumptions on key exchange hash algorithm and output
   length, preparing OpenSSH for KEX methods with alternate hashes.

 * Ignore junk sent by a server before  it sends the "SSH-" banner
   (Bugzilla #1067)

 * The manpages has been significantly improves and rearranged, in 
   addition to other specific manpage fixes:
   #1037 - Man page entries for -L and -R should mention -g.
   #1077 - Descriptions for "ssh -D" and DynamicForward should mention
           they can specify "bind_address" optionally.
   #1088 - Incorrect descriptions in ssh_config man page for 
           ControlMaster=no.
   #1121 - Several corrections for ssh_agent manpages

 * Lots of cleanups, including fixes to memory leaks on error paths
   (Bugzilla #1109, #1110, #1111 and more) and possible crashes (#1092)

 * Portable OpenSSH-specific fixes:

     processing of new connections on platforms using the OpenSSH's
     builtin entropy collector (ssh-rand-helper)

     #1045 - Missing option for ignoring the /etc/nologin file
     #1087 - Show PAM password expiry message from LDAP on login
     #1028 - Forward final non-query conversations to client
     #1126 - Prevent user from being forced to change an expired
             password repeatedly on AIX in some PAM configurations.
     #1045 - Do not check /etc/nologin when PAM is enabled, instead 
             allow PAM to handle it.  Note that on platforms using 
             PAM, the pam_nologin module should be used in sshd's 
             session stack in order to maintain past behaviour

     #989  - Fix multiplexing regress test on Solaris
     #1097 - Cross-compile fixes.
     #1096 - ssh-keygen broken on HPUX.
     #1098 - $MAIL being set incorrectly for HPUX server login.
     #1104 - Compile error on Tru64 Unix 4.0f
     #1106 - Updated .spec file and startup for SuSE.
     #1122 - Use _GNU_SOURCE define in favor of __USE_GNU, fixing
             compilation problems on glibc 2.4

Changes since OpenSSH 4.1:
============================ 

  - SECURITY: Fix a bug introduced in OpenSSH 4.0 that caused 
    GatewayPorts to be incorrectly activated for dynamic ("-D") port 
    forwardings when no listen address was explicitly specified.

  - SECURITY: sshd in OpenSSH versions prior to 4.2 allow GSSAPI 
    credentials to be delegated to users who log in with methods 
    other than GSSAPI authentication (e.g. public key) when the 
    client requests it. This behaviour has been changed in OpenSSH 
    4.2 to only delegate credentials to users who authenticate
    using the GSSAPI method. This eliminates the risk of credentials 
    being inadvertently exposed to an untrusted user/host (though 
    users should not activate GSSAPIDelegateCredentials to begin
    with when the remote user or host is untrusted)

  - Added a new compression method that delays the start of zlib
    compression until the user has been authenticated successfully. 
    The new method ("Compression delayed") is on by default in the 
    server. This eliminates the risk of any zlib vulnerability 
    leading to a compromise of the server from unauthenticated users.

    NB. Older OpenSSH (<3.5) versions have a bug that will cause them
    to refuse to connect to any server that does not offer compression
    when the client has compression requested. Since the new "delayed"
    server mode isn't supported by these older clients, they will
    refuse to connect to a new server unless compression is disabled
    (on the client end) or the original compression method is enabled
    on the server ("Compression yes" in sshd_config)

  - Another round of proactive changes for signed vs unsigned integer
    bugs has been completed, including changing the atomicio() API to
    encourage safer programming. This work is ongoing.

  - Added support for the improved arcfour cipher modes from
    draft-harris-ssh-arcfour-fixes-02. The improves the cipher's
    resistance to a number of attacks by discarding early keystream
    output.

  - Increase the default size of new RSA/DSA keys generated by
    ssh-keygen from 1024 to 2048 bits.

  - Many bugfixes and improvements to connection multiplexing,
    including:

    - Added ControlMaster=auto/autoask options to support opportunistic
      multiplexing (see the ssh_config(5) manpage for details).

    - The client will now gracefully fallback to starting a new TCP
      connection if it cannot connect to a specified multiplexing
      control socket

    - Added %h (target hostname), %p (target port) and %r (remote
      username) expansion sequences to ControlPath. Also allow
      ControlPath=none to disable connection multiplexing.

    - Implemented support for X11 and agent forwarding over multiplexed
      connections. Because of protocol limitations, the slave
      connections inherit the master's DISPLAY and SSH_AUTH_SOCK rather
      than distinctly forwarding their own.

  - Portable OpenSSH: Added support for long passwords (> 8-char) on
    UnixWare 7.

  - The following bugs from http://bugzilla.mindrot.org/ were closed:

     #471  - Misleading error message if /dev/tty perms wrong
     #623  - Don't use $HOME in manpages
     #829  - Don't allocate a tty if -n option is set
     #1025 - Correctly handle disabled special character in ttymodes
     #1033 - Fix compile-time warnings
     #1046 - AIX 5.3 Garbage on Login
     #1054 - Don't terminate connection on getpeername() failure
     #1076 - GSSAPIDelegateCredentials issue mentioned above

  - Lots of other improvements and fixes. Please refer to the ChangeLog
    for details

Thanks to everyone who has contributed patches, problem or test reports.

Changes since OpenSSH 4.0:
============================ 

* This is a bugfix release, no new features have been added. Some notable
  fixes are:

  - Fix segfault when using forwardings configured in ssh_config(5) and 
    ClearAllForwardings (bugzilla #996)

  - Limit input buffer size for channels. A peer could send more data
    than the buffer code was willing to accept. This would cause OpenSSH
    to abort the connection (bugzilla #896)

* Several improvements to the regression tests

* Portable OpenSSH:

  - OpenSSH will now always normalise IPv4 in IPv6 mapped addresses back to 
    IPv4 addresses. This means that IPv4 addresses in log messages on IPv6
    enabled machines will no longer be prefixed by "::ffff:" and AllowUsers,
    DenyUsers, AllowGroups, DenyGroups will match IPv4-style addresses only 
    for 4-in-6 mapped connections. This ensures a consistent representation
    of IPv4 addresses regardless of whether or not the machine is IPv6
    enabled.

* Other bugfixes, including bugzilla #950, #997, #998, #999, #1005, #1006, 
  #1024, and #1038

Changes since OpenSSH 3.9:
============================ 

* ssh(1) now allows the optional specification of an address to bind to 
  in port forwarding connections (local, remote and dynamic). Please 
  refer to the documentation for the -L and -R options in the ssh(1) 
  manual page and the LocalForward and RemoteForward options in the 
  ssh_config(5) manpage. (Bugzilla #413)

* To control remote bindings while retaining backwards compatibility,
  sshd(8)'s GatewayPorts option has been extended. To allow client
  specified bind addresses for remote (-R) port forwardings, the server
  must be configured with "GatewayPorts clientspecified".

* ssh(1) and ssh-keyscan(1) now support hashing of host names and 
  addresses added to known_hosts files, controlled by the ssh(1) 
  HashKnownHosts configuration directive. This option improves user 
  privacy by hiding which hosts have been visited. At present this 
  option is off by default, but may be turned on once it receives 
  sufficient testing.

* Added options for managing keys in known_hosts files to ssh-keygen(1),
  including the ability to search for hosts by name, delete hosts by
  name and convert an unhashed known_hosts file into one with hashed
  names. These are particularly useful for managing known_hosts files
  with hashed hostnames.

* Improve account and password expiry support in sshd(8). The server
  will now warn in advance for both account and password expiry.

* sshd(8) will now log the source of connections denied by AllowUsers,
  DenyUsers, AllowGroups and DenyGroups (Bugzilla #909)

* Added AddressFamily option to sshd(8) to allow global control over
  IPv4/IPv6 usage. (Bugzilla #989)

* Improved sftp(1) client, including bugfixes and optimisations for the 
  ``ls'' command and command history and editing support using libedit.

* Improved the handling of bad data in authorized_keys files,
  eliminating fatal errors on corrupt or very large keys. (Bugzilla
  #884)

* Improved connection multiplexing support in ssh(1). Several bugs 
  have been fixed and a new "command mode" has been added to allow the
  control of a running multiplexing master connection, including 
  checking that it is up, determining its PID and asking it to exit.

* Have scp(1) and sftp(1) wait for the spawned ssh to exit before they
  exit themselves.  This prevents ssh from being unable to restore 
  terminal modes (not normally a problem on OpenBSD but common with 
  -Portable on POSIX platforms). (Bugzilla #950)

* Portable OpenSSH:

  - Add *EXPERIMENTAL* BSM audit support for Solaris systems 
    (Bugzilla #125)

  - Enable IPv6 on AIX where possible (see README.platform for
    details), working around a misfeature of AIX's getnameinfo. 
    (Bugzilla #835)

  - Teach sshd(8) to write failed login records to btmp for
    unsuccessful auth attempts. Currently this is only for password,
    keyboard-interactive and challenge/response authentication methods
    and only on Linux and HP-UX.

  - sshd(8) now sends output from failing PAM session modules to the 
    user before exiting, similar to the way /etc/nologin is handled

  - Store credentials from gssapi-with-mic authentication early enough
    to be available to PAM session modules when privsep=yes.

Changes since OpenSSH 3.8:
============================ 

* Added new "IdentitiesOnly" option to ssh(1), which specifies that it should
  use keys specified in ssh_config, rather than any keys in ssh-agent(1)

* Make sshd(8) re-execute itself on accepting a new connection. This security
  measure ensures that all execute-time randomisations are reapplied for each 
  connection rather than once, for the master process' lifetime. This includes
  mmap and malloc mappings, shared library addressing, shared library mapping 
  order, ProPolice and StackGhost cookies on systems that support such things

* Add strict permission and ownership checks to programs reading ~/.ssh/config
  NB ssh(1) will now exit instead of trying to process a config with poor 
  ownership or permissions

* Implemented the ability to pass selected environment variables between the
  client and the server. See "AcceptEnv" in sshd_config(5) and "SendEnv" in 
  ssh_config(5) for details
 
* Added a "MaxAuthTries" option to sshd(8), allowing control over the maximum
  number of authentication attempts permitted per connection

* Added support for cancellation of active remote port forwarding sessions. 
  This may be performed using the ~C escape character, see "Escape Characters"
  in ssh(1) for details
 
* Many sftp(1) interface improvements, including greatly enhanced "ls" support 
  and the ability to cancel active transfers using SIGINT (^C)

* Implement session multiplexing: a single ssh(1) connection can now carry 
  multiple login/command/file transfer sessions. Refer to the "ControlMaster" 
  and "ControlPath" options in ssh_config(5) for more information

* The sftp-server has improved support for non-POSIX filesystems (e.g. FAT)

* Portable OpenSSH: Re-introduce support for PAM password authentication, in 
  addition to the keyboard-interactive driver. PAM password authentication 
  is less flexible, and doesn't support pre-authentication password expiry but
  runs in-process so Kerberos tokens, etc are retained

* Improved and more extensive regression tests

* Many bugfixes and small improvements

Changes since OpenSSH 3.7.1:
============================ 

* sshd(8) now supports forced changes of expired passwords via
  /usr/bin/passwd or keyboard-interactive authentication.

  keep-alive messages to the server.  See ServerAliveInterval
  in ssh(1) for more information.

  protocol version 2.

  Please see README.dns in the source distribution for details.

* Fix a number of memory leaks.

* The experimental "gssapi" support has been replaced with
  the "gssapi-with-mic" to fix possible MITM attacks.
  The two versions are not compatible.

Security Changes:
=================

  Portable OpenSSH version 3.7p1 and 3.7.1p1 contain multiple 
  vulnerabilities in the new PAM authentication code. At least one of
  these bugs is remotely exploitable (under a non-standard 
  configuration, with privsep disabled).

  OpenSSH 3.7.1p2 fixes these bugs. Please note that these bugs do not 
  exist in OpenBSD's releases of OpenSSH.

Changes since OpenSSH 3.7.1p1:
==============================

* This release disables PAM by default. To enable it, set "UsePAM yes" in 
  sshd_config. Due to complexity, inconsistencies in the specification and
  differences between vendors' PAM implementations we recommend that PAM 
  be left disabled in sshd_config unless there is a need for its use. 
  Sites using only public key or simple password authentication usually 
  have little need to enable PAM support.

* This release now requires zlib 1.1.4 to build correctly. Previous 
  versions have security problems.

* Fix compilation for versions of OpenSSL before 0.9.6. Some cipher modes 
  are not supported for older OpenSSL versions.

* Fix compilation problems on systems with a missing or lacking inet_ntoa()
  function.

* Workaround problems related to unimplemented or broken setresuid/setreuid 
  functions on several platforms.

* Fix compilation on older OpenBSD systems.

* Fix handling of password-less authentication (PermitEmptyPasswords=yes) 
  that has not worked since the 3.7p1 release.

Changes since OpenSSH 3.6.1:
============================ 

* The entire OpenSSH code-base has undergone a license review. As
  a result, all non-ssh1.x code is under a BSD-style license with no
  advertising requirement. Please refer to README in the source
  distribution for the exact license terms.

* Rhosts authentication has been removed in ssh(1) and sshd(8).

* Changes in Kerberos support:

    - KerberosV password support now uses a file cache instead of
      a memory cache.

    - KerberosIV and AFS support has been removed.

    - KerberosV support has been removed from SSH protocol 1.

    - KerberosV password authentication support remains for SSH
      protocols 1 and 2.

    - This release contains some GSSAPI user authentication support
      to replace legacy KerberosV authentication support. At present
      this code is still considered experimental and SHOULD NOT BE
      USED.
  
* Changed order that keys are tried in public key authentication.
  The ssh(1) client tries the keys in the following order:

     1. ssh-agent(1) keys that are found in the ssh_config(5) file
     2. remaining ssh-agent(1) keys
     3. keys that are only listed in the ssh_config(5) file

  This helps when an ssh-agent(1) has many keys, where the sshd(8)
  server might close the connection before the correct key is tried.

* SOCKS5 support has been added to the dynamic forwarding mode
  in ssh(1).

* Removed implementation barriers to operation of SSH over SCTP.

* sftp(1) client can now transfer files with quote characters in
  their filenames.

* Replaced sshd(8)'s VerifyReverseMapping with UseDNS option.
  When UseDNS option is on, reverse hostname lookups are always
  performed.

* Fix a number of memory leaks.

* Support for sending tty BREAK over SSH protocol 2.

* Workaround for other vendor bugs in KEX guess handling.

* Support for generating KEX-GEX groups (/etc/moduli) in ssh-keygen(1).

* Automatic re-keying based on amount of data sent over connection.

* New AddressFamily option on client to select protocol to use (IPv4
  or IPv6).

* Experimental support for the "aes128-ctr", "aes192-ctr", and
  "aes256-ctr" ciphers for SSH protocol 2.

* Experimental support for host keys in DNS (draft-ietf-secsh-dns-xx.txt).
  Please see README.dns in the source distribution for details.

* Portable OpenSSH:

    - Replace PAM password authentication kludge with a more correct
      PAM challenge-response module from FreeBSD.

    - PAM support may now be enabled/disabled at runtime using the
      UsePAM directive.

    - Many improvements to the OpenSC smartcard support.

    - Regression tests now work with portable OpenSSH.
      Please refer to regress/README.regress in the source distribution.

    - On platforms that support it, portable OpenSSH now honors the
      UMASK, PATH and SUPATH attributes set in /etc/default/login.

    - Deny access to locked accounts, regardless of authentication
      method in use.

Changes between OpenSSH 3.5 and OpenSSH 3.6:
============================================

* RSA blinding is now used by ssh(1), sshd(8) and ssh-agent(1).
  in order to avoid potential timing attacks against the RSA keys.
  Older versions of OpenSSH have been using RSA blinding in
  ssh-keysign(1) only.

  Please note that there is no evidence that the SSH protocol is
  vulnerable to the OpenSSL/TLS timing attack described in
        http://crypto.stanford.edu/~dabo/papers/ssl-timing.pdf

* ssh-agent(1) optionally requires user confirmation if a key gets
  used, see '-c' in ssh-add(1).

* sshd(8) now handles PermitRootLogin correctly when UsePrivilegeSeparation
  is enabled.

* sshd(8) now removes X11 cookies when a session gets closed.

* ssh-keysign(8) is disabled by default and only enabled if the
  new EnableSSHKeysign option is set in the global ssh_config(5)
  file.

* ssh(1) and sshd(8) now handle 'kex guesses' correctly (key exchange
  guesses).

* ssh(1) no longer overwrites SIG_IGN.  This matches behaviour from
  rsh(1) and is used by backup tools.

* setting ProxyCommand to 'none' disables the proxy feature, see
  ssh_config(5).

* scp(1) supports add -1 and -2.

* scp(1) supports bandwidth limiting.

* sftp(1) displays a progressmeter.

* sftp(1) has improved error handling for scripting.

Changes since OpenSSH 3.4:
============================ 

* Improved support for Privilege Separation (Portability, Kerberos,
  PermitRootLogin handling).

* ssh(1) prints out all known host keys for a host if it receives an
  unknown host key of a different type.

* Fixed AES/Rijndael EVP integration for OpenSSL < 0.9.7 (caused
  problems with bounds checking patches for gcc).

* ssh-keysign(8) is disabled by default and only enabled if the
  HostbasedAuthentication option is enabled in the global ssh_config(5)
  file.

* ssh-keysign(8) uses RSA blinding in order to avoid timing attacks
  against the RSA host key.

* A use-after-free bug was fixed in ssh-keysign(8).  This bug
  broke hostbased authentication on several platforms.

* ssh-agent(1) is now installed setgid in order to avoid ptrace(2)
  attacks.

* ssh-agent(1) now restricts the access with getpeereid(2) (or
  equivalent, where available).

* sshd(8) no longer uses the ASN.1 parsing code from libcrypto when
  verifying RSA signatures.

* sshd(8) now sets the SSH_CONNECTION environment variable.

* Enhanced "ls" support for the sftp(1) client, including globbing and
  detailed listings.

* ssh(1) now always falls back to uncompressed sessions, if the
  server does not support compression.

* The default behavior of sshd(8) with regard to user settable
  environ variables has changed:  the new option PermitUserEnvironment
  is disabled by default, see sshd_config(5).

* The default value for LoginGraceTime has been changed from 600 to 120
  seconds, see sshd_config(5).

* Removed erroneous SO_LINGER handling.

OpenSSH 3.0.2 was released on 2002-12-04. It is available from the

implementation and includes sftp client and server support.

Important Changes:
==================

        This release fixes a vulnerability in the UseLogin option
        of OpenSSH.  This option is not enabled in the default
        installation of OpenSSH.

        However, if UseLogin is enabled by the administrator, all
        versions of OpenSSH prior to 3.0.2 may be vulnerable to
        local attacks.

        The vulnerability allows local users to pass environment
        variables (e.g. LD_PRELOAD) to the login process.  The login
        process is run with the same privilege as sshd (usually
        with root privilege).

        Do not enable UseLogin on your machines or disable UseLogin
        again in /etc/sshd_config:
		UseLogin no

We also have received many reports about attacks against the crc32
bug.  This bug has been fixed about 12 months ago in OpenSSH 2.3.0.
However, these attacks cause non-vulnerable daemons to chew a lot
of cpu since the crc32 attack sends a tremendously large amount of
data which must be processed.

OpenSSH 3.0.1/3.0.1p1 (2001-11-19)

OpenSSH 3.0.1 was released on 2001-11-19. It is available from the
mirrors listed at https://www.openssh.com/.
OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol version 1.3, 1.5 and 2.0
implementation and includes sftp client and server support.

We would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their continued
support and encouragement.

Important Changes:
==================

        A security hole that may allow an attacker to authenticate
        if -- and only if -- the administrator has enabled KerberosV.
        By default, OpenSSH KerberosV support only becomes active
        after KerberosV has been properly configured.

        An excessive memory clearing bug (which we believe to be
        unexploitable) also exists, but since this may cause daemon
        crashes, we are providing a fix as well.

        Various other non-critical fixes (~& support and more).

OpenSSH is brought to you by Markus Friedl, Niels Provos, Theo de Raadt,
Kevin Steves, Damien Miller and Ben Lindstrom.

OpenSSH 3.0/3.0p1 (2001-11-06)

OpenSSH 3.0 was released on 2001-11-06. It is available from the
mirrors listed at https://www.openssh.com/.
OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol version 1.3, 1.5 and 2.0
implementation and includes sftp client and server support.

This release contains many portability bug-fixes (listed in the
ChangeLog) as well as several new features (listed below).

We would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their continued
support and encouragement.

Important Changes:
==================

1) SSH protocol v2 is now the default protocol version

	use the 'Protocol' option from ssh(1) and sshd(8) if
	you need to change this.

2) The files
	/etc/ssh_known_hosts2
	~/.ssh/known_hosts2
	~/.ssh/authorized_keys2
   are now obsolete, you can use
	/etc/ssh_known_hosts
	~/.ssh/known_hosts
	~/.ssh/authorized_keys
   For backward compatibility ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 will still used for
   authentication and hostkeys are still read from the known_hosts2.
   However, those deprecated files are considered 'readonly'.  Future
   releases are likely not to read these files.

3) The CheckMail option in sshd_config is deprecated, as sshd(8) no longer
   checks for new mail.

4) X11 cookies are now stored in $HOME.

New Features:
=============

1) Smartcard support in the ssh client and agent based on work by
   University of Michigan CITI (http://www.citi.umich.edu/projects/smartcard/).
2) support for Rekeying in protocol version 2

3) improved Kerberos support in protocol v1 (KerbIV and KerbV)

4) backward compatibility with older commercial SSH versions >= 2.0.10

5) getopt(3) is now used by all programs

6) dynamic forwarding (use ssh(1) as your socks server)

7) ClearAllForwardings in ssh(1)

8) ssh(1) now checks the hostkey for localhost (NoHostAuthenticationForLocalhost yes/no).

9) -F option in ssh(1)

10) ssh(1) now has a '-b bindaddress' option

11) scp(1) allows "scp /file localhost:/file"

12) The AuthorizedKeysFile option allows specification of alternative
    files that contain the public keys that can be used for user authentication
    (e.g. /etc/ssh_keys/%u, see sshd(8))

13) extended AllowUsers user@host syntax in sshd(8)

14) improved challenge-response support (especially for systems supporting BSD_AUTH)

15) sshd(8) can specify time args as 1h, 2h30s etc.

16) sshd(8) transmits the correct exit status for remote execution with protocol version 2.

17) ssh-keygen(1) can import private RSA/DSA keys generated with the commercial version

18) ssh-keyscan(1) supports protocol version 2

OpenSSH is brought to you by Markus Friedl, Niels Provos, Theo de Raadt,
Kevin Steves, Damien Miller and Ben Lindstrom.

OpenSSH 2.9.9/2.9.9p1 (2001-09-25)

OpenSSH 2.9.9 has just been uploaded. It is available from the
mirrors listed at https://www.openssh.com/.
OpenSSH 2.9.9 fixes a weakness in the key file option handling,
including source IP based access control.

OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol version 1.3, 1.5 and 2.0
implementation and includes sftp client and server support.

This release contains many portability bug-fixes (listed in the
ChangeLog) as well as several new features (listed below).

We would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their continued
support and encouragement.

Security Notes:
===============

This release fixes weakness in the source IP based access control
for SSH protocol v2 public key authentication:

        Versions of OpenSSH between 2.5 and 2.9.9 are
        affected if they use the 'from=' key file option in
        combination with both RSA and DSA keys in
        ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2.

        Depending on the order of the user keys in
        ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 sshd might fail to apply the
        source IP based access control restriction (e.g.
        from="10.0.0.1") to the correct key:

        If a source IP restricted key (e.g. DSA key) is
        immediately followed by a key of a different type
        (e.g. RSA key), then key options for the second key
        are applied to both keys, which includes 'from='.

	This means that users can circumvent the system policy
	and login from disallowed source IP addresses.
	

Important Changes:
==================

OpenSSH 2.9.9 might have upgrade issues introduced by the long time
between releases, which may affect people in unforeseen ways:

1) The files
	/etc/ssh_known_hosts2
	~/.ssh/known_hosts2
	~/.ssh/authorized_keys2
   are now obsolete, you can use
	/etc/ssh_known_hosts
	~/.ssh/known_hosts
	~/.ssh/authorized_keys
   For backward compatibility ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 is still used for
   authentication and hostkeys are still read from the known_hosts2.
   However, old files are considered 'readonly'.  Future releases are
   likely to not read these files.

2) The CheckMail option in sshd_config is deprecated, sshd no longer
   checks for new mail.

3) X11 cookies are stored in $HOME

OpenSSH 2.5.2p2 (2001-03-22)

Portable OpenSSH 2.5.2p2 is now available from the mirror sites
listed at http://www.openssh.com/portable.html

Security related changes:
	Improved countermeasure against "Passive Analysis of SSH
	(Secure Shell) Traffic"
	http://openwall.com/advisories/OW-003-ssh-traffic-analysis.txt

	The countermeasures introduced in earlier OpenSSH-2.5.x versions
	caused interoperability problems with some other implementations.

	Improved countermeasure against "SSH protocol 1.5 session
	key recovery vulnerability"
	http://www.core-sdi.com/advisories/ssh1_sessionkey_recovery.htm

New options:
	permitopen authorized_keys option to restrict portforwarding.

	PreferredAuthentications allows client to specify the order in which
	authentication methods are tried.

Sftp:
	sftp client supports globbing (get *, put *).

	Support for sftp protocol v3 (draft-ietf-secsh-filexfer-01.txt).

	Batch file (-b) support for automated transfers

Performance:
	Speedup DH exchange. OpenSSH should now be significantly faster when
	connecting use SSH protocol 2.

	Preferred SSH protocol 2 cipher is AES with hmac-md5. AES offers
	much faster throughput in a well scrutinised cipher.

Bugfixes:
	stderr handling fixes in SSH protocol 2.

	Improved interoperability.

Client:
	The client no longer asks for the passphrase if the key
	will not be accepted by the server (SSH2_MSG_USERAUTH_PK_OK)

Miscellaneous:
	scp should now work for files > 2GB

	ssh-keygen can now generate fingerprints in the "bubble babble"
	format for exchanging fingerprints with SSH.COM's SSH protocol 2
	implementation.

Portable version:
	Better support for the PRNGd[1] entropy collection daemon. The
	--with-egd-pool configure option has been deprecated in favour
	of --with-prngd-socket and the new --with-prngd-port options.
	The latter allows collection of entropy from a localhost
	socket.

	configure ensures that scp is in the $PATH set by the server
	(unless a custom path is specified).

[1] http://www.aet.tu-cottbus.de/personen/jaenicke/postfix_tls/prngd.html

OpenSSH 2.5.1p1 (2001-02-19)

Portable OpenSSH 2.5.1p1 has just been uploaded. It will be available 
from the mirrors listed at http://www.openssh.com/portable.html shortly.

OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH 1.3 & 1.5 protocol implementation and 
a 99% SSH 2 protocol implementation, including sftp client and server
support.

This release contains many portability bug-fixes (listed in the
ChangeLog) as well as several new features (listed below).

OpenSSH 2.5.0p1 was skipped because of interoperability issues with 
ssh-1.2.18 => ssh-1.2.22.

We would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their continued support
and encouragement.

Important Changes:
==================

1) Features added to the implementation of the SSH 2 protocol:

    * agent forwarding
    * support for -R forwarding
    * RSA host and userkeys
    * extended support for older SSH 2 protocol implementations

    OpenSSH still lacks support for rekeying, so you have to turn off
    rekeying if your server tries to force this feature.

    The next release of OpenSSH will probably support rekeying.

2) Damien Miller contributed an interactive sftp client.

    The sftp client works for both SSH protocol versions.

3) David Mazieres' ssh-keyscan has been added to the OpenSSH distribution.

4) Now there are three types of keys in OpenSSH:

    RSA1 is used by the SSH 1 protocol only,
    RSA and DSA keys are used by the SSH 2 protocol implementation.

    You can generate RSA keys for use with SSH 2 protocol with:

        $ ssh-keygen -t rsa -f /etc/ssh_host_rsa_key

        To use RSA or DSA keys in SSH 2 protocol, simply
        add the public keys to the .ssh/authorised_keys2 file.

    IdentityFile2, HostDsaKey and DSAAuthentication are obsolete:

    You can use multiple IdentityFile and HostKey options instead, e.g
        HostKey /etc/ssh_host_key
        HostKey /etc/ssh_host_dsa_key
        HostKey /etc/ssh_host_rsa_key
    in /etc/sshd_config

    The option DSAAuthentication has been replaced by PubkeyAuthentication.

    Fingerprinting works for all types of keys:

        $ ssh-keygen -l -f $HOME/.ssh/{authorized_keys,known_hosts}{,2}

5) Important changes in the implementation of SSH 1 protocol:

    The OpenSSH server does not require a privileged source port for
    RhostsRsaAuthentication, since it adds no additional security.

    Interoperation with SSH 1.4 protocol

6) New option HostKeyAlias

    This option allows the user to record the host key under a
    different name. This is useful for tunneling over
    forwarded connections or if you run multiple sshd's on
    different ports on the same machine.

    Alternatively you can use the UserKnownHostsFile or 
    UserKnownHostsFile2 options to specify separate host key
    files for the connection.

7) The ReverseMappingCheck is now optional in sshd_config.

    If you combine this with the 'sshd -u0' option the server
    will not do DNS lookups when a client connects.

8) Stricter Hostkey Checking

9) Option Change Summary:

    a) New or changed:

        ChallengeResponseAuthentication
        MACs
        PubkeyAuthentication

        HostkeyAlias        (Client only)

        Banner              (Server only)
        ReverseMappingCheck (Server only)

        PermitRootLogin     {yes,without-password,forced-commands-only,no}

        {Allow,Deny}Groups  now support supplementary groups

        sshd -D             for monitoring scripts or inittab
        ssh -t              multiple -t force tty allocation

    b) Obsolete:

        DsaAuthentication   (use PubkeyAuthentication instead)
        HostDsaKey          (use HostKey)
        Identityfile2       (use Identityfile or -i)
        SkeyAuthentication  (use ChallengeResponseAuthentication)
        TisAuthentication   (use ChallengeResponseAuthentication)

OpenSSH is brought to you by Markus Friedl, Niels Provos, Theo de Raadt,
Kevin Steves, Damien Miller and Ben Lindstrom.

course.

  addresses) in wtmp when `UseLogin' is set to `yes'. (Markus Friedl)

- Fix problems when sshd is run from inetd

  Tamito KAJIYAMA)

  Garrick James)
- Further improved NeXT support. (Ben Lindstrom, Mark Miller)
- Lots of other minor fixes (see ChangeLog for details)

This release has been tested on HPUX (10.20, 11.00), Irix (5.3,

OpenServer 5.0.5, Solaris 2.7 (Sparc), Solaris 2.8 (i386, Sparc),
SNI/Reliant Unix, DEC OSF/Tru64 5.0.

time.

The 2.1.1p3 release of portable OpenSSH has been uploaded to the
OpenBSD ftp master site. In a few hours it will be available from one
of the many mirrors listed at:

fixes.

OpenSSH 2.1.1p2 (2000-07-01)

Announcing the release of portable OpenSSH 2.1.1p2.

This release primarily contains fixes to the bugs that have been
reported over the last month, in particular:

 - Invalid time bring written to utmp/wtmp on systems using bash2

 - Several lastlog fixes

 - AIX, SCO, Irix portability fixes

 - Avoid failures on PAM systems when using PAM authentication modules
   which require a tty.

 - Entropy collection fixes for Solaris.

 - EGD robustness improvements

 - Fixes and enhancements from the OpenBSD team:
   - Fixed options processing in authorized_keys2 file
   - Compatibility with commercial SSH 2.0.13 and 2.2.0
   - Numerous minor fixes

There are also a couple of new features:

 - Shadow password expiry support (no password change support yet)

 - Irix 6.x array sessions, project IDs and system audit trail IDs

 - Beginnings of Tru64 / OSF SIA (Security Integration Architecture) 
   support

 - Beginnings of NeXT support

Version 2.1.1p2 will be available from the mirrors listed at
http://www.openssh.com/portable.html (as soon as they update).

Many thanks to all those who tested the snapshots and/or contributed
bug reports and patches

Regards,
Damien Miller

OpenSSH 2.1.1p1 (2000-06-09)

Announcing the availability of portable OpenSSH 2.1.1p1.

This release contains the fix for the "UseLogin yes" vulnerability
identified in Markus' release and several other enhancements and
bugfixes. Including:

 - Better login code. Andre Lucas has rewritten the login code to 
   be much more modular and extensible. In the process he has fixed 
   the problems with Solaris utmp[x].

 - Revised the entropy collection code to be faster and more reliable.

 - Fix for RSA host restrictions ("from=" in authorized_keys)

It is recommended that all users upgrade to this version.

Portable OpenSSH 2.1.1p1 is available from one of the many mirrors
listed at: http://www.openssh.com/portable.html

Regards,
Damien Miller

OpenSSH 2.1.0p1 (2000-05-09)

This is to announce the release of openssh-2.1.0, the first stable
release of portable OpenSSH to incorporate support for the SSH2
protocol.

The SSH2 protocol offers a number of advantages over the SSH1 protocol
including standards compliance (SSH2 is on the IETF standards
track[1]), improved security and operation without RSA (which is
patented in some countries).

The SSH2 support in OpenSSH has been developed by Markus Friedl, with
support from the OpenBSD team.

This is also the first version of the portable version of OpenSSH
to offer built-in entropy collection. This removes the requirement
for EGD on systems that lack a /dev/random driver. As a result,
OpenSSH-2.1.0 now requires a recent version of OpenSSL[2] to compile
(version 0.9.5 or later).

NB. The portable version of OpenSSH is currently in the
process of merging its webpages with the official OpenBSD
project. Please use http://www.openssh.com/ from now
on. Distribution files are also available from the mirrors listed at
http://violet.ibs.com.au/openssh/files/MIRRORS.html

Please read http://www.openssh.com/report.html before reporting bugs.
Patches, bug reports, developer and user queries are welcome on the
mailing list (http://www.openssh.com/list.html).
Regards,
Damien Miller

item.title: Awesome repositories are no longer awesome (156 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://erikgahner.github.io/posts/2026/awesome-repositories-are-no-longer-awesome/, See on Hacker News

On GitHub, you will find a lot of repositories with the prefix 'awesome'. They usually contain curated knowledge and resources related to a certain domain, such as awesome-python (see, e.g., this repository for a list of awesome repositories). I used to see these awesome repositories as potential goldmines of good content. However, nowadays I see most of them as irrelevant and useless. There are two reasons for this, and they are both related to AI.

First, as many of these awesome lists get older, they contain a lot of outdated material if they are not actively maintained. You are in most cases better off simply asking a decent AI model for inspiration or the material you need. That is, I find it difficult to believe that most of these awesome lists are of interest to people anymore. If they remain useful, it will mostly be for agents looking to find and check relevant resources.

I had a quick look at the awesome-R repository. The repository was last updated more than a year ago, and most of the resources included in the overview are either outdated or will not be of general interest to people using R. One of the first links in the repository is an overview of the top 50 downloaded packages - as of 2016! This is simply not a good resource if you want to explore R in any shape or form.

Second, a lot of these awesome repositories are being flooded with AI slop. Go to any random awesome repository these days and you will most likely find a lot of pull requests suggesting the most generic tools and resources. For example, take a look at this awesome-free-online-tools repository. It is a small, unknown repository with 13 stars but 91 open pull requests at the time of writing. I did not look at all of these pull requests, but the ones I looked at all suggested generic vibe-coded tools.

I found this resource because of a pull request made to one of my repositories, a simple project where I store material I like related to statistics. The suggestion was to add StatOrigin ("a free, open database of industry statistics"), and once I had a quick look at the resource and the other pull requests made by the user, I could easily close the PR. This user alone has created at least six vibe-coded websites (StatOrigin, ScanChess, Sticker Printer Hub, QuizQuip, LiquidityPools, DefiLPKit) and submitted more than 100 pull requests to various awesome lists to add these websites.

It did not take me long to find examples where these tools were merged into the relevant repositories (see, e.g., here, here, and here). However, I also found examples where people did the basic work of checking out the material, such as here, where the PR was closed with the following explanation: "There is not yet sufficient evidence of qualified educator review, independent validation of the educational content, or demonstrated learning outcomes." Good stuff!

My point is not that these awesome repositories are now all bad. They can still be awesome. But as a general approach to finding good resources, awesome lists are less awesome than they used to be. As AI gets better at finding and creating resources (and creating pull requests for said resources), these awesome repositories will become less relevant and less useful.

item.title: Baidu released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base (121 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ernie.baidu.com/release/ernie-5-5-flash-base/, See on Hacker News

Table of Contents
01Introduction02Model Architecture03Pre-training04Evaluation05Quick Start06Conclusion and Outlook07Citation

1. Introduction

A base model is valuable both for the capabilities that pre-training builds and for the starting point it offers for further training. Different domains, reasoning tasks and agentic applications call for different data, training objectives and behaviors. Releasing the weights at the end of pre-training lets developers build on the general capabilities already in place and choose for themselves where to take the model next.

Today we are releasing ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model with 280B total parameters, 14B of which are activated per token. It was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens with a training context of up to 128K, and supports a 1M-token context for fine-tuning and inference. The weights are the checkpoint at the end of pre-training, before any mid- or post-training, and can serve as a common starting point for domain adaptation, instruction tuning and reinforcement-learning research.

To be worth building on, a base model has to stay affordable to train and run, so efficiency was a design goal from the outset. Further training samples from the model repeatedly, and agentic applications bring multi-turn interactions and long contexts. Both add to compute and memory costs. ERNIE 5.5 Flash therefore revisits the trade-off between capability and efficiency in every component, from attention and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, and weighs activated compute, KV cache and long-context cost together rather than one at a time.

The same thinking shaped the data and the training system. Every later stage of training builds on what pre-training provides, so the corpus emphasizes capabilities that are hard to add afterwards, such as repository-scale code and long-context understanding. And because an efficient architecture pays off only if it can also be trained efficiently at scale, we designed the model and the training system together.

We hope this release spares more developers the cost of large-scale pre-training, so they can spend their own resources on the capabilities, tasks and training methods they care about.

Key highlights:

  • An open starting point for further training. Base weights with no mid- or post-training, leaving the community free to pursue its own approaches to domain adaptation, reasoning and agent training.
  • Built for efficient further training and inference. Sparse MoE and hybrid sparse attention balance model capacity, activated compute and long-context cost in the architecture itself.
  • Broad data, efficient training. Diverse, high-quality pre-training data gives later training a well-rounded foundation, and a training system co-designed with the architecture keeps large-scale pre-training efficient.
  • A clean research baseline. A single checkpoint taken at the end of pre-training makes it easy to compare training methods under controlled conditions and to measure what each one adds.

2. Model Architecture

ERNIE 5.5 Flash has 43 Transformer layers, a hidden size of 4096 and 64 attention heads.

2.1 Latent-Gated Sparse Attention

Hybrid MLA + HCA attention: Most layers need only a coarse view of the distant past, so only one layer in seven keeps token-level access to the full context, using Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). The remaining layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA): each compresses every 128 tokens into a single cached entry, then attends to all of these entries plus a short window of recent, uncompressed tokens. An HCA layer therefore still sees the whole sequence, while caching only a small fraction of what a full-context layer needs.

Layer-specific head dimensions: Instead of using the same head dimension in every layer, we set it according to how expensive each layer's attention is: cheap layers get wide heads, expensive layers get narrower ones. HCA layers attend over a sequence compressed 128×, so their attention is cheap and they can afford wide 512-dim heads at little extra compute. MLA layers attend at token level and cost more, so they use narrower 256-dim heads for both query/key and value.

Concentrating the KV-cache budget on MLA layers: With HCA in most layers, the main question is where to spend the rest of the KV-cache budget. One option is many Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) layers, which compress the history 4× and attend only to a selected part of it. We instead use a few MLA layers that keep every token. In our pre-training comparisons at a similar KV-cache budget, HCA combined with MLA outperforms HCA combined with CSA.

Sparse attention in the full-context layers: The MLA layers are the only layers that see every distant token individually. With dense attention, they would account for most of the attention compute at long context lengths, so they use sparse attention (DSA) instead. A lightweight indexer scores past positions for each query, and core attention is computed only over the top-k highest-scoring positions. The per-query cost of core attention therefore stays constant as the context grows. With DSA, these layers match dense attention in pre-training loss and train substantially faster.

Two further changes apply inside the attention layers:

  • Low-Rank Gated Attention: Gated attention multiplies the attention output by a learned gate, which has been shown to improve both quality and training stability. Normally the gate is computed from the layer's hidden state. We instead compute it from the low-rank query latent, a compressed form of the query that each attention layer already computes. Because this latent is 4× narrower than the hidden state, the gate projection has 75% fewer weights, and our ablations also show better performance. Every attention layer in ERNIE 5.5 Flash, MLA and HCA alike, uses Low-Rank Gated Attention.
  • Virtual Head Attention (VHA): After attention, VHA adds a lightweight low-rank mixing step across heads, with an identity skip connection. This lets heads share information, which improves expressiveness and training quality, and at inference it is fused into the attention kernel with negligible overhead.

2.2 Multi-Router Latent MoE

A conventional MoE layer picks experts with a single router and a hard top-k. We find that a single router's scores correlate only weakly with how useful each expert actually is, especially in the middle and deeper layers. And because experts left out of the top-k receive no gradient from that token, the router gets no signal that it chose wrongly, so wrong selections tend to reinforce themselves.

Multi-Router replaces the single router with several independently initialized sigmoid routers that score the experts jointly. The routers develop clearly distinct preferences: an expert can be chosen because one router strongly favors it or because several favor it together, so a wrong choice is easier to correct. The errors of any one router no longer decide the selection, and routing becomes less sensitive to noisy features and distribution shift. The number of activated experts, expert FLOPs and communication volume stay the same. Compared with a single router, routing scores correlate noticeably better with how useful each expert is, with the largest gains in the middle and deeper layers.

All layers except the first use an MoE feed-forward block:

  • 512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared expert, with auxiliary-loss-free, bias-corrected load balancing.
  • Latent experts. Each MoE layer first projects tokens from 4096 to a 2048-d latent space; the experts (intermediate size 2048) run in that space, and a single shared up-projection maps the result back to 4096. This roughly halves dispatch/combine traffic and expert FLOPs relative to full-width experts.
  • Stable LatentMoE design with learnable scalars. The MoE blocks follow the Stable LatentMoE design (an RMSNorm before the up-projection and SiTU-GLU expert activations), which keeps expert outputs well scaled across all 43 layers and stabilizes optimization. In addition, each routed expert's routing weight is multiplied by its own learnable scalar.

2.3 Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC)

ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the standard residual connection with mHC: each layer reads from and writes to 4 parallel residual streams through a constrained mixing matrix, which gives layers a wider channel for passing information to one another at negligible extra compute.

2.4 MultiMax Output Head

A single softmax temperature forces a trade-off: lowering it makes the distribution sparse but also suppresses other plausible tokens; raising it keeps them but fattens the long tail of implausible ones. MultiMax replaces the single temperature with a learnable piecewise temperature, so the output head no longer has to choose: it suppresses the long tail of implausible tokens while keeping several plausible next tokens. The logits are rescaled element-wise inside the chunked, Triton-fused cross-entropy kernel just before the softmax. This adds negligible training overhead and no extra memory, and significantly lowers pre-training loss.

2.5 ECHO: Replacing the MTP Module

Conventional multi-token prediction (MTP) attaches extra modules to the backbone to predict future tokens, so the loss on future tokens mostly trains those modules, and the backbone is still trained mainly to predict the next token. ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the MTP module with ECHO, which reuses the backbone's own final layer to predict future tokens. Because there is no separate MTP layer, the loss on future tokens directly trains the same parameters that produce the next token. Learning to look past the next token encourages the backbone to anticipate where the sequence is heading, with clear gains on reasoning and code. ERNIE 5.5 Flash is pre-trained with single-step ECHO. The same layer also serves as the draft model for speculative decoding, and it generalizes beyond its training: although trained to predict only one extra token, it drafts several tokens ahead, with a higher acceptance rate than an auxiliary MTP module trained the same way.

2.6 Tokenizer

ERNIE 5.5 Flash uses a new BPE tokenizer with a vocabulary of about 200K entries. Numbers are tokenized right-to-left (R2L) in groups of up to three digits, so that digits with the same place value line up across numbers of different lengths (e.g. 1,234,567 → 1 234 567). This helps with arithmetic and number-heavy text.

3. Pre-training

ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens with the Muon optimizer and FP8 mixed precision. The training context was gradually extended to 128K tokens over the course of pre-training, and fine-tuning and inference support a 1M-token context. The released checkpoint is taken at the end of pre-training and has not gone through any mid-training or post-training.

3.1 Data

The pre-training corpus covers a wide range of domains and languages and is curated for both breadth of knowledge and quality. Beyond this broad base, we focused on three areas:

  • Web data. Multilingual web data is crawled at scale, extracted with high fidelity and filtered by models that score quality along several dimensions. The result covers a broad range of knowledge and is dense in useful training signal.
  • Code data. Code collected from repositories and the web is filtered to remove non-code content, aggressively deduplicated and graded for quality at several granularities. Beyond static code, the corpus includes data on how software evolves and executes: commits, issues, pull requests, code reviews, requirement-to-PR and multi-commit trajectories, generated tests and CI-verified fixes. This data targets repository-level reasoning and agentic software engineering.
  • Long-context data. Three complementary sources: natural long documents, selected for long-range dependencies and cleaned with embedding-based deduplication, LLM quality scoring and rules; long sequences built by concatenating natural texts with retrieved, semantically similar distractors; and synthetic data for MRCR-style retrieval, citation-grounded QA and multi-hop QA.

3.2 Training Infrastructure

We built two infrastructure components for this run: a distributed Muon optimizer that stays efficient across thousands of GPUs, and FlashMask-4, an attention kernel for large head dimensions.

Distributed Muon. Unlike element-wise optimizers such as Adam, Muon orthogonalizes the update of each parameter matrix as a whole. This changes how distributed training communicates and how memory is spread across GPUs. Two optimizations make it practical at the scale of thousands of GPUs:

  • Communication-efficient updates. Conventionally, dense parameters are synchronized over a single ring that passes through every GPU in the cluster. Data travels across a long chain of inter-node links in many small messages, which leaves the links underused, and latency and jitter grow as the cluster gets larger. MoE parameters are synchronized differently: each GPU exchanges data only with the GPUs that hold the same rank on other nodes. We move dense-parameter synchronization onto this same path and combine the dense and MoE transfers into one collective operation. Messages become larger, so bandwidth is used more fully; the communication pattern becomes more regular and fits expert-parallel communication; and inter-node latency and jitter drop significantly. The optimizer's updates stay exactly the same.
  • Memory-balanced sharding. Muon needs large messages to communicate efficiently, so naive sharding groups many parameter tensors together and places them on the first few GPUs. A handful of nodes then hold far more optimizer state than the rest. They are prone to OOM failures and slow to save, upload and download checkpoints, which lengthens failure recovery, and the problem grows with GPU count. Our inter-node balanced sharding spreads these optimizer states over more GPUs, including those later in the order. Memory is then balanced almost evenly across nodes, while messages stay large enough for efficient communication.

FlashMask-4 for large head dimensions. At large head dimensions, FlashAttention-style kernels run up against the limits of on-chip storage such as shared memory and tensor memory: compute utilization drops, and some configurations are hard to implement at all. FlashMask-4 is built on CuTe-DSL for both SM90 and SM100 GPUs. It works around these limits with 2-CTA tiled parallel computation and, on SM100, double-buffer rotation in tensor memory. It keeps FlashMask's compact O(N) column-wise mask representation and still skips fully masked blocks. It supports head dimensions up to qk_head_dim = 576 and v_head_dim = 512, beyond what FlashAttention-4 supports. On SM100 GPUs, it is up to 175% faster in the forward pass and up to 74% faster in the backward pass than FlashAttention-4 MaskMod.

4. Evaluation

4.1 Setup

For comparison, we selected the latest open-source base models of similar size publicly available at the time of release: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B-A13B), Hy3-preview-Base (295B-A21A) and MiMo-V2.5-Base (310B-A15B). All four models are evaluated from their publicly released checkpoints with the same evaluation harness, prompts and few-shot examples, and with the same LLM judge for free-form QA.

4.2 Overall Results

ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base performs strongly across all benchmark categories, with reasoning, code and exam benchmarks among its best results. Although 37 of the 43 layers attend over a sequence compressed 128×, the six MLA-DSA layers are enough to keep performance strong on the six long-context benchmarks.

4.3 Detailed Results

The best result in each row is shown in bold. Swipe horizontally on mobile to view the full table.

5. Quick Start

ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base is available on Hugging Face in FP8 and BF16 safetensors (the BF16 version is ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base-BF16), under the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0. The model expects a BOS token at the start of every input, so keep add_special_tokens=True when tokenizing.

Python · Transformers

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch

model_name = "baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base-BF16"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")
model_inputs = tokenizer(["The hybrid attention architecture of ERNIE 5.5 Flash"], add_special_tokens=True, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
print(tokenizer.decode(model.generate(**model_inputs, max_new_tokens=256)[0], skip_special_tokens=True))

SGLang and vLLM both serve the model through the completions API; see the model card for deployment instructions. For fine-tuning, please refer to the ERNIE 5.5 example.

6. Conclusion and Outlook

ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base starts from one premise: a base model meant for further training should be efficient by design. We balanced capability and efficiency in every component, from attention and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head. The architecture is backed by broad, high-quality pre-training data and by a training system designed together with the model. With 14B parameters activated per token and a compact KV cache, the model performs strongly across a broad range of benchmarks, including long-context ones.

This base model is only a starting point. The post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash will follow, and we look forward to seeing what the community builds on top of it, whether for domain adaptation, reasoning or agents.

Citation

If you find ERNIE 5.5 useful in your research or projects, please consider citing this blog post:

item.title: Lemmings CSS Animation (304 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://markblah.github.io/lemmings/, See on Hacker News

Add walkers with the button below or __walker.add(). Drag one to carry it, flick it to throw it. Resize the window and walkers ride the surface they're standing on, so a fast resize launches them.

Stairs

Stairs too tall to climb

Floating platforms

Pit

Walls

Cards

These wrap onto new rows as the window narrows, which shoves anyone standing on them.

Card one

Borders are solid. Walk the top edge or get trapped inside.

Card two

Buttons and form fields are solid too.

Card three

Text is a floor you can land on but walk through.

Card four

Throw a walker up here.

Cage

Reading

Columns of text reflow a lot when the window changes size, so this is a good place to try a resize launch. Each line of text is its own floor. Walkers can drop from line to line, fall off the end of a short line, and land on whatever is below.

Lines sit closer together than a walker is tall, so text never blocks them. Only borders, boxes, buttons, images and fields do. That keeps walkers from getting stuck between two lines of a paragraph.

Near the bottom of the page there is one long floor to catch anything that falls all the way down.

item.title: Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor Part 3: Bad Update Improvements (132 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://icode4.coffee/?p=1746, See on Hacker News

Welcome to part 3 of the Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor blog series. In this part I’ll go over what happened after I released the PoC for Bad Update, and how it went from taking ~20 minutes with a ~30% success rate to being near instantaneous with a near 100% success rate. If you haven’t already I highly recommend you read (or at least skim through) part 1 and part 2 as this post will reference a lot of the material discussed there. This part will be very short but will catch you up for part 4 which covers the peer pressure exploit and will be out soon.

Rock Band Blitz

In the months following the release of Bad Update v1.0 there were two major improvements made to it by others. The first by “ihatecompvir” and “InvoxiPlayGames” is a new game save entry point in the demo version of Rock Band Blitz (RBB) called DaTArrest. The demo version of RBB is a package file that’s normally downloaded from the Xbox Live store for free and saved to your console’s HDD or memory unit. When the Xbox 360 got support for using USB sticks as storage devices all of the packages signed to boot from the HDD or memory unit were grandfathered in to also boot from USB storage devices. This means the RBB demo package can be copied to a USB stick as a normal file and launched on any console on a software version that supports it.

By exploiting some memory corruption vulnerabilities in the game’s DLC parsing code they were able to craft a game save file that when loaded would bootstrap the Bad Update stage 2 ROP chain and begin the hypervisor exploit chain. Using RBB as an entry point we no longer needed the Tony Hawk American Wasteland game disc. Running the Bad Update exploit was now as simple as copying some files to a USB stick, plugging it into your console, and launching Rock Band Blitz from the dashboard.

Hypervisor Race Condition Optimizations

Shortly after the RBB entry point was discovered I received a pull request from “Máté” who had made some improvements to the hypervisor race condition part of the exploit. These improvements included a hash table for precomputing and storing the malicious ciphertext values, a better cache flushing primitive, and improved thread scheduling between the XKE payload thread and ciphertext overwrite thread. The combination of these improvements reduced execution time down to a few seconds and the race condition had a much higher success rate.

Ciphertext Hash Table

In part 2 I talked about attacking encrypted memory by using hypervisor APIs to create encrypted memory allocations at predetermined memory addresses and used two different memory pathways to capture the ciphertext for some chosen plaintext data. Using this primitive I was able to craft ciphertext data to get kernel mode code execution as well as the ciphertext data used to attack the LZX decompression code in the bootloader update XKE payload.

The whitening value used in the memory encryption scheme is 12 bits large which gives 1024 unique ciphertext combinations for some given plaintext data. However, in my original PoC I was only generating the ciphertext for one of the 1024 possible whitening values and the reason for that was a two part failure on my end. When I originally prototyped out the ciphertext attack I did actually try using a lookup table for ciphertext combinations but I wasn’t able to get it working.

The first issue was I was using a very old ~2011 era hypervisor/kernel build (it was just what all my old research was based on) which was doing a TLB flush for the encrypted VA range in the hypervisor function that setup the memory encryption. In later hypervisor builds that TLB flush was removed because the kernel wrapper function for this hypervisor function already does a TLB flush for the VA range. However, I call the hypervisor syscall directly (skipping the kernel wrapper code which does the TLB flush) and since the TLB is lazy-loaded the whitening bits would become stale and the resulting ciphertext read out of memory was invalid.

When testing the exploit on the 17559 (latest) version hypervisor the lookup table was causing issues and rather than investigate I decided I’d fix it later and moved on. By the time I got to the end of the exploit I had become so blinded by tunnel vision chasing CPU cache issues that I had convinced myself the lookup table just wasn’t going to work. What I should have probably done (aside from investigate the lookup table issues when they surfaced) was to put this project down for a few weeks and come back with a clear mindset. Oh well, lesson learned…

Getting into the implementation details of the hash table, we use the first N bits of the ciphertext we expect to see in memory as an index into two arrays. The first array contains the first 64-bits of the oracle ciphertext which is used for validation in case there’s ever a collision in the hash table. The second array stores our malicious ciphertext we want to write into memory.

// Index bits of the ciphertext lookup pseudo-hashtable

#define HASH_BITS 20

struct CIPHER_TEXT_DATA

{

    ULONGLONG dec_end_input_pos;

    ULONGLONG dec_output_buffer;                            // New dec_output_buffer pointer (dst address for memcpy)

    ULONGLONG OracleCipherText[1 << HASH_BITS];             // Cipher text for the LZX decoder context header, used to detect when to start the race attack

    ULONGLONG ReplacementCipherText1[1 << HASH_BITS];       // Cipher text containing our malicious dec_output_buffer pointer (points to hypervisor memory)

    ULONGLONG ReplacementCipherText2[1 << HASH_BITS];

};

In order to make this as efficient as possible (remember we’re racing the CPU and cache here) we ignore collisions. It’s better to have a few collisions and have to skip some iterations on the race condition loop than to implement support for buckets in the hash table. Instead we compensate for collisions by choosing a sufficiently large enough number of bits for the hash table key such that the number of collisions is on the order of single digits, if we even have any (majority of the time there’s 0).

However, more bits in the hash table key means a large array to hold the entries (meaning more memory is used) which could potentially work against us as we’ll be performing more fetches from RAM since CPU cache is being thrashed. Máté’s original PR used a key size of 10 bits but I later upped this to 20 bits which seems to be a happy spot where there’s usually no collisions or if there are it’s a low single digit number. The total size of memory needed to hold both hash tables is about 24MB.

void BuildCipherTextLookupTable(BYTE* pUpdateData, DWORD UpdateDataSize, DWORD ScratchOffset, CIPHER_TEXT_DATA* pCipherTextData)

{

    // Arbitrary virtual address that will get mapped through the encrypted pathway to BaseAddrPhys.

    BYTE *pMemoryAddress = (BYTE*)0x8D000000;

    ...

    // Scan all 1024 possible whitening bits.

    for (int i = 0; i < 1024; i++)

    {

        // Allocate encrypted memory.

        HvxEncryptedReserveAllocation((DWORD)pMemoryAddress, BaseAddrPhys, UpdateDataSize);

        HvxEncryptedEncryptAllocation((DWORD)pMemoryAddress);

        // Manually flush the TLB entry for the encrypted allocation address so we pick up the new whitening value.

        HvxFlushSingleTb(pMemoryAddress);

        // Get the cipher text for the expected header data in the LZX decoder context. This acts as a

        // trigger to know when to start the race attack.

        memset(pMemoryAddress, 0, 16);

        *(ULONG*)(pMemoryAddress + 0) = 0x4349444c;     // signature = 'CIDL'

        *(ULONG*)(pMemoryAddress + 4) = 0x8000;         // windows size = 0x8000

        *(ULONG*)(pMemoryAddress + 8) = 1;              // cpu type = 1

        __dcbst(0, (char *) pMemoryAddress);

        KeFlushCacheRange(pMemoryAddress, 0x80);

        KeFlushCacheRange(pUpdateData + ScratchOffset, 0x80);

        // Use the first N bits of the cipher text data as an index into the lookup table.

        ULONGLONG oracleData = *(ULONGLONG *)(pUpdateData + ScratchOffset);

        int index = oracleData >> (64 - HASH_BITS);

        // Check if we hit a collision in the cipher text lookup table.

        if (pCipherTextData->OracleCipherText[index] != 0)

            collisionCount++;

        // Add the current cipher text entry to the lookup table, overwriting any existing value.

        pCipherTextData->OracleCipherText[index] = oracleData;

        // Get the corresponding cipher text for our malicious dec_output_buffer pointer which points to the hypervisor code we want to overwrite.

        *(ULONGLONG*)(pMemoryAddress + 0x2B20) = pCipherTextData->dec_end_input_pos;

        *(ULONGLONG*)(pMemoryAddress + 0x2B28) = pCipherTextData->dec_output_buffer;

        __dcbst(0, (char *) pMemoryAddress + 0x2B00);

        KeFlushCacheRange(pMemoryAddress + 0x2B00, 0x80);

        KeFlushCacheRange(pUpdateData + ScratchOffset + 0x2B00, 0x80);

        // Store cipher text for our malicious dec_output_buffer pointer into the lookup table.

        pCipherTextData->ReplacementCipherText1[index] = *(ULONGLONG *) (pUpdateData + ScratchOffset + 0x2B20);

        pCipherTextData->ReplacementCipherText2[index] = *(ULONGLONG *) (pUpdateData + ScratchOffset + 0x2B28);

        // Free the encrypted allocation.

        result = HvxEncryptedReleaseAllocation((DWORD)pMemoryAddress);

    }

}

Looking at the snippet above we can see how the hash table is built. We loop 1024 times to exhaust all possible whitening values for this page of memory. Each iteration we encrypt the page (which will increment the whitening value), get the ciphertext for the LZX decoder data we expect to be in memory and the ciphertext for our malicious data, then add them to the hash tables. On lines 15-16 we can see the HvxFlushSingleTb call that thwarted my own attempt at using a hash table, and on lines 30-31 we can see how the first N bits of the expected ciphertext is used as the hash table key.

Improved Cache Flushing

In my original PoC I used a unique feature of the Xbox 360 CPU to lock away half of the available L2 cache to try and put as much pressure on it as I could. The L2 locking technique was pivotal in the original PoC but it didn’t put as much pressure on CPU cache as I would have liked. Putting pressure on CPU cache is particularly annoying because kernel mode (where the exploit code is running) cannot use certain cache flushing instructions due to them being privileged and only usable in hypervisor mode.

Additionally, the hypervisor only runs with CPU caching enabled when operating on encrypted memory which makes finding a hypervisor level cache flush primitive difficult. I tried to work around this by finding a hypervisor syscall that would read a large amount of encrypted memory, and I did find one syscall that fit the description, but it wasn’t nearly enough for what I needed. That function also had locks in it which prevented me from executing it on multiple threads simultaneously.

However, there was a kernel mode cache instruction I completely overlooked that Máté had found to work extremely well, dcbz or data cache block set to zero. Aside from just zero’ing out a CPU cache line this instruction has an interesting side effect:

If the cache block is already in the data cache, all of its bytes are cleared to zero. If it is not in the cache, the block is allocated and initialized directly in the cache to zero without reading the old contents from main memory.

So if this instruction is used on a memory address that’s not currently in CPU cache the CPU will allocate space for it and potentially evict something else to make room for it. By running the dcbz instruction over large regions of memory it can be used as a cache flush primitive and force old data in CPU cache to be evicted. In Máté’s original implementation he allocated an 0x80000 byte region of memory then looped over it and for every 0x80 bytes (the size of a cache line) called dcbz.

This worked extremely well, however, I found that by increasing the allocation size by 3x and calling dcbz at three distinct locations I was able to assert slightly more pressure on CPU cache which would be important for another improvement I’ll get to later on. Here’s the final implementation:

void CacheThrashThreadProc(THREAD_ARGS* pArgs)

{

    // Allocate a scratch buffer to help with thrashing L2 cache.

    BYTE* pCacheThrashBuffer = (BYTE*)MmAllocatePhysicalMemoryEx(MEM_REGION_TITLE, 0x180000, PAGE_READWRITE | MEM_LARGE_PAGES, NULL, MAXULONG_PTR, 0x20000);

    BYTE* pCacheThrashBuffer2 = pCacheThrashBuffer + 0x80000;

    BYTE* pCacheThrashBuffer3 = pCacheThrashBuffer + 0x100000;

    // Loop until we're told to exit.

    while (pArgs->bRunCacheThrashing != FALSE)

    {

        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)

        {

            // Walk the entire scratch buffer and try to fetch it into CPU cache.

            int offset = 0;

            while (offset < 0x80000)

            {

                // Zero three distinct blocks.

                __dcbz(offset, pCacheThrashBuffer);

                __dcbz(offset, pCacheThrashBuffer2);

                __dcbz(offset, pCacheThrashBuffer3);

                offset += 0x80;

            }

        }

    }

}

Improved Thread Scheduling

In part 2 I talked about trying to schedule the exploit threads on different hardware threads and how I got the best results by putting them on CPU hardware threads 0 and 1 (which are both on core 0). I don’t really know anything about how CPUs work at a hardware level but I suspected that the load/store memory transactions from both hardware threads on the same core were being queued onto the L2 crossbar in some sort of per-core fashion. Thus by putting the exploit threads on the hardware threads for a single core the writes from the exploit thread and reads from the XKE payload thread would get queued together and reduce latency for loads/stores to RAM, or something like that.

It’s probably not very surprising to anyone reading this but CPUs often have “hidden” instructions, ones not defined by the instruction set architecture (ISA) but implemented by the CPU manufacturer. Sometimes these have a special instruction encoding and other times you’d use an existing instruction in a nonsensical way to tell the CPU to do a special operation.

In the case of PowerPC the ISA actually has some well defined instructions for changing the priority of a hardware thread by executing a special OR instruction with all 3 register operands set to the same specific register based on what priority you want the hardware thread to run at. For example:

or      r1, r1, r1      # Low priority

or      r2, r2, r2      # Medium priority

or      r5, r5, r5      # High priority

The Xbox 360 SDK docs describe a few intrinsic macros that can be used to set the priority of the hardware thread the code is running on: __SetHWThreadPriorityLow, __SetHWThreadPriorityMed, and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh. The actual CPU instructions used by these macros are slightly different than what I listed above (these macros are xenon CPU specific) but that doesn’t really matter.

The SDK docs describe every core as having 32 dispatch slots which are split evenly between hardware threads running at medium priority (which is the default priority). By using the __SetHWThreadPriorityLow and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh intrinsic macros you can have one hardware thread use 31 of the 32 dispatch slots and the other only use 1. How the dispatch slots relate to number of instructions fed to the CPU execution units I’m not sure (again I have no idea how a CPU pipeline actually works), but being able to go from 16/16 to 1/31 sounds pretty handy for scheduling the exploit threads.

Using these intrinsic macros Máté was able to schedule the exploit threads such that the hardware thread running the XKE payload was only getting 1 of the 32 dispatch slots while the ciphertext overwrite thread got the remaining 31 slots. The result was that the CPU was now spending the overwhelming majority of time in the ciphertext detection loop than it was actually running the XKE payload.

Improved Ciphertext Overwrite Detection

The last improvement was something I came up with while working on the Peer Pressure exploit to try and make the Bad Update exploit as stable as I could get it. In the original PoC I had discovered the compressed bootloader data the XKE payload operates on was compressed into 15 blocks with all but the last block having a decompressed size of 0x8000 bytes. If the XKE payload attack was successful part of the last segment of the hypervisor would be overwritten with the decompressed data for one or more of the compressed blocks. By observing the ciphertext for the last segment of the hypervisor in two distinct locations I could determine if the last block of compressed data was written to it by the XKE payload.

The attack was setup such that if the last block of compressed data was written to the hypervisor at a specific offset it would change the instructions for one of hypervisor syscalls to a write-what-where primitive I could use to get full hypervisor code execution. However, there was a flaw in how the ciphertext was being observed which not only led to false positives that would crash the console but also missed iterations where the last block was written to memory successfully.
